To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the joint projections of temperature change and precipitation change from the climate models used by the IPCC in their latest report on climate change projections are not consistent with each other and are also not consistent with the observed climate, and that the uncertainty in these projections is very high, as is reflected in the large posterior variance of the climate change projections.

(1) the projections of future climate change from the climate models that were used in the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report are consistent, in a statistical sense, with the current observed climate, and (2) the projections of climate change that we obtain from a statistical analysis of the model simulations and the observations are in agreement with the projections that are obtained from the climate models alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantification of the uncertainties in future climate projections and the development of a statistical framework that can help to represent these uncertainties in a transparent way.

the quantification of uncertainty and variability in future climate projections, which is of vital importance for impact studies, and we have developed and demonstrated a statistical method for this purpose.

the quantification of the uncertain nature of climate change projections from general circulation models (GCMs), in terms of the future projections of temperature and of precipitation, and the uncertainties in the model projections are quantified by a Bayesian hierarchical model that fully characterizes a rich set of parameters, including biases, correlation terms, model-specific precisions and trends.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results from our analysis are in line with the results that were reported in the IPCC report, but with the important difference that our analysis fully characterizes the uncertain nature of climate projections, and that our results are not limited to the mean projections.

the results of the present study indicate that the climate models are able to reproduce the current climate reasonably well, but they do not agree well with each other, nor are the projections of climate change consistent.
the results from this paper show that the climate models used by the IPCC for the 4th assessment report are not yet sufficiently reliable to provide a sound basis for impact studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a statistical methodology to represent the uncertainty in climate model projections in terms of posterior predictive distributions of the climate signal.
our Bayesian analysis has shown that there is a high probability of future changes in the climate that are not only significant, but also large enough to have major impacts on the Earth system.

it is possible to quantify the uncertainty in climate model projections of temperature and of precipitation, and that it is important to do so in order to be able to assess the impacts of climate change in a meaningful way.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the uncertainties in climate model projections are large.

we have demonstrated that a hierarchical Bayesian approach to climate model projections can be used to obtain a more complete representation of uncertainty in climate projections than is typically done in climate change studies.
the uncertainties in climate model projections can be represented by the posterior distributions of a hierarchical model that we have proposed.
